notes.definition: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms and are strong.
explanation: When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. Covalent bonding happens between non-metal atoms. Each shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nuclei of both atoms, and this holds the atoms together. These bonds between atoms are strong. By sharing, each atom usually gains a full outer shell: hydrogen needs a share in 2 electrons, and most other non-metals need 8. One shared pair is a single bond, two shared pairs make a double bond (as in O₂) and three shared pairs make a triple bond (as in N₂).

Covalently bonded substances can have three kinds of structure. Many consist of small molecules, such as hydrogen (H₂), chlorine (Cl₂), oxygen (O₂), nitrogen (N₂), hydrogen chloride (HCl), water (H₂O), ammonia (NH₃), methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Some have very large molecules, such as polymers like poly(ethene). Some have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide (SiO₂), in which a huge number of atoms are joined by covalent bonds in a continuous network. You can usually recognise a small molecule from its formula: it is made only of non-metals and has a small, fixed number of atoms, for example H₂O or NH₃.

Dot and cross diagrams show the outer shell electrons of each atom, with electrons from one atom as dots and from the other as crosses. Shared pairs are drawn in the overlap between the atoms' shells. Electrons that are not shared, called lone pairs, are drawn in pairs on the outer shell. You should be able to draw dot and cross diagrams for H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃ and CH₄. A quick check: carbon forms 4 bonds, nitrogen 3, oxygen 2, and hydrogen and chlorine 1 each.

Covalent bonds can also be shown as lines, where each line represents one single bond (a shared pair of electrons). This is used in displayed formulae of small molecules (H–Cl, O=O, N≡N), in the repeating units of polymers, and in diagrams of part of a giant covalent structure. A repeating unit of a polymer is drawn in brackets with bonds passing through the brackets and an n outside, which shows that the unit repeats many times. You should be able to deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a model or diagram by counting the atoms of each element, for example a model with 2 carbon atoms, 6 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom gives C₂H₆O.

Each type of diagram has limitations. Dot and cross diagrams show which atom the electrons came from and how many bonds form, but they do not show the shape of the molecule or the relative sizes of atoms, and they suggest electrons from different atoms are different, when all electrons are identical. Displayed formulae show which atoms are bonded, but not the 3D shape or the lone pairs. Ball and stick models show the 3D shape and bond angles, but bonds are not sticks, atoms are much closer together than shown, and electrons are not shown. 3D space-filling models show the shape and relative sizes of atoms, but it is hard to see the bonds and how many there are. Diagrams of giant structures show only a tiny part of the structure.
keyFacts: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two (non-metal) atoms.
Covalent substances may be small molecules, very large molecules (polymers) or giant covalent structures (diamond, silicon dioxide).
Single bond = 1 shared pair; double bond = 2 shared pairs (O₂); triple bond = 3 shared pairs (N₂).
C forms 4 bonds, N forms 3, O forms 2, H and Cl form 1.
Lone pairs are pairs of outer electrons that are not shared.
In displayed formulae each line represents one covalent bond.
Polymer repeating units are drawn in brackets with an n, with bonds extending through the brackets.
Molecular formula is found by counting each type of atom in a model of the molecule.
Every type of diagram (dot and cross, displayed, ball and stick, 3D) has limitations.

keyTerms.definition: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A particle made of two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds.
A pair of outer shell electrons that is not involved in bonding.
Two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms, shown as =.
Three shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms, shown as ≡.
A diagram showing all the atoms in a molecule and every covalent bond as a line.
A very large number of atoms joined by covalent bonds in a continuous network, such as diamond or silicon dioxide.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule, for example C₂H₆O.
The section of a polymer chain that repeats many times, drawn in brackets with n.

workedExamples.title: Dot and cross diagram for ammonia
workedExamples.question: Describe how to draw a dot and cross diagram for ammonia, NH₃.
steps: Nitrogen is 2,5, so it has 5 outer electrons (draw as dots). Each hydrogen has 1 electron (draw as a cross).
Nitrogen needs 3 more electrons, so it shares one pair with each of 3 hydrogen atoms.
Draw the N circle overlapping three H circles. In each overlap put one dot and one cross.
Nitrogen has 2 electrons left over: draw them as one lone pair (two dots) on the N outer shell.
Check: N has 8 outer electrons (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair) and each H has 2.
workedExamples.answer: Three shared pairs (• ×) between N and each H, plus one lone pair of dots on nitrogen.

workedExamples.title: Molecular formula from a model
workedExamples.question: A ball and stick model shows 3 carbon atoms (black) and 8 hydrogen atoms (white), all joined by single bonds. Give the molecular formula and the number of covalent bonds.
steps: Count each type of atom: C = 3, H = 8.
Bonds: each H forms 1 bond, so 8 C–H bonds. The 3 carbons are in a chain, joined by 2 C–C bonds.

workedExamples.title: Recognising small molecules from formulae
workedExamples.question: Which of these consist of small molecules: CO₂, NaCl, SiO₂, NH₃, Cu, Cl₂?
steps: Small molecules contain only non-metals and have a small fixed number of atoms.
NaCl contains a metal, so it is ionic. Cu is a metal.
SiO₂ is made of non-metals, but it is a giant covalent structure (the formula is a ratio, not a molecule).
CO₂, NH₃ and Cl₂ are small molecules.

diagrams.title: Other ways to represent covalent bonds
diagrams.caption: A displayed formula and a ball and stick model of methane, the repeating unit of poly(ethene), and a flat sketch of part of a giant covalent structure. Each line represents one covalent bond.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think covalent bonds are weak because many covalent substances are gases.
misconceptions.right: Covalent bonds are strong. Small molecules have low boiling points because the forces between molecules are weak.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the dots and crosses are different kinds of electron.
misconceptions.right: All electrons are identical; dots and crosses just show which atom each electron came from.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw oxygen (O₂) with a single bond.
misconceptions.right: Each oxygen atom needs 2 more electrons, so O₂ has a double bond (two shared pairs) and each O has two lone pairs.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all covalent substances are small molecules.
misconceptions.right: Some are giant covalent structures (diamond, silicon dioxide) and some are very large molecules (polymers).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget lone pairs on N, O and Cl atoms.
misconceptions.right: Every atom except hydrogen should end with 8 outer electrons, including any lone pairs.

realWorld: Nitrogen's triple bond is very strong, which is why N₂ in the air is unreactive and fertiliser production needs the Haber process.
Poly(ethene) plastic bags and bottles are made of very long covalently bonded molecules.
Chemists use ball and stick and space-filling computer models to design medicines that fit target molecules in the body.
examTips: In dot and cross diagrams, put shared pairs in the overlap, include all lone pairs, and check every atom (except H) has 8 outer electrons and each H has 2.
Only draw outer shells unless asked, and use dots for one element and crosses for the other.
Count bonds using valency: C 4, N 3, O 2, H 1, Cl 1. This helps you draw displayed formulae correctly.
For polymer repeating units, the bonds must pass through the brackets and n goes at the bottom right outside the bracket.
When asked for a limitation, name the specific thing the model does not show (3D shape, relative size, electrons, that bonds are not sticks).
summary: Covalent bonds are shared pairs of electrons between non-metal atoms, and they are strong.
Covalent substances can be small molecules, large molecules (polymers) or giant covalent structures.
Learn dot and cross diagrams for H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃ and CH₄.
A line represents a single covalent bond in displayed formulae, polymer repeating units and giant structures.
Every representation has limitations; know what each shows and does not show.
Find a molecular formula by counting the atoms in a model.

questions.question: What is a covalent bond?
options: The attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The transfer of an electron from one atom to another
The attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are shared pairs of electrons. The other options describe ionic bonding, electron transfer and metallic bonding.

questions.question: Which substance consists of small molecules?
markScheme: 1 mark: Ammonia
questions.explanation: Ammonia (NH₃) is a small molecule. Diamond and silicon dioxide are giant covalent structures; sodium chloride is ionic.

questions.question: How many covalent bonds are there in a molecule of methane, CH₄?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and shares one with each of 4 hydrogen atoms, forming 4 single C–H bonds.

questions.question: Which type of bond is in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: Triple bond
questions.explanation: Each N atom has 5 outer electrons and needs 3 more, so the atoms share three pairs: N≡N.

questions.question: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the oxygen atom in a water molecule?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons. Two are used in the two O–H bonds, leaving 4 electrons as 2 lone pairs, giving 8 in total.

questions.question: Which substance is an example of a giant covalent structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Silicon dioxide
questions.explanation: Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) is a giant covalent structure. CO₂ and CH₄ are small molecules; poly(ethene) has very large molecules but is not giant covalent.

questions.question: In a dot and cross diagram of hydrogen chloride, how many electrons are in the outer shell of the chlorine atom (including shared electrons)?
markScheme: 1 mark: 8
questions.explanation: Chlorine has 7 of its own outer electrons plus 1 from hydrogen in the shared pair, giving 8 (one shared pair and three lone pairs).

questions.question: A model of a molecule shows 2 carbon atoms, 4 hydrogen atoms and a double bond between the carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?
markScheme: 1 mark: C₂H₄
questions.explanation: Count the atoms: 2 C and 4 H gives C₂H₄ (ethene). CH₂ is the simplest ratio, not the molecular formula.

questions.question: Which is a limitation of a ball and stick model of methane?
options: It shows the 3D shape of the molecule.
It shows which atoms are bonded together.
It shows the bonds as sticks, but bonds are shared pairs of electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: It shows the bonds as sticks, but bonds are shared pairs of electrons.
questions.explanation: Bonds are not physical sticks; they are shared electron pairs, and the model also exaggerates the distance between atoms. The other options are strengths.

questions.question: Element Z forms a molecule ZH₃ with one lone pair on Z. Which group is Z in?
markScheme: 1 mark: Group 5
questions.explanation: Z uses 3 electrons in bonds and has 2 in a lone pair: 5 outer electrons, so Group 5 (like nitrogen in NH₃).

questions.question: Which statement about the representation of the repeating unit of poly(ethene) is correct?
options: The brackets show that the molecule is ionic.
The bonds through the brackets show the chain continues on both sides.
n shows the number of carbon atoms in each unit.
Each line represents a pair of shared atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: The bonds through the brackets show the chain continues on both sides.
questions.explanation: The bonds that pass through the brackets link to the next repeating units. n is the number of repeats; each line is one shared pair of electrons.

questions.question: How many covalent bonds does an ammonia molecule, NH₃, contain?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3
questions.explanation: Nitrogen shares one pair with each of the three hydrogen atoms: three N–H single bonds.

questions.question: How many electrons are shared between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6
questions.explanation: A triple bond is three shared pairs, which is 3 × 2 = 6 electrons.

questions.question: How many non-bonding (lone pair) electrons are there in total in a chlorine molecule, Cl₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12
questions.explanation: Each Cl has 7 outer electrons, 1 of which is used in the shared pair. That leaves 6 (three lone pairs) on each atom: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.question: A ball and stick model of a molecule shows 2 carbon atoms, 6 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, all joined by single bonds (C, C, O in a chain: C–C–O–H). How many covalent bonds are in the molecule?
markScheme: 1 mark: 5 C–H bonds + 1 C–C + 1 C–O + 1 O–H
1 mark: 8
questions.explanation: This is ethanol, C₂H₆O (CH₃CH₂OH). It has 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bond = 8. Check with valencies: (2 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 6 × 1) ÷ 2 = 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.question: State what is meant by a covalent bond.
markScheme: 1 mark: a shared pair of electrons (between two atoms)
questions.explanation: The word 'pair' and the idea of sharing are both needed.

questions.question: Give two examples of substances that consist of small covalent molecules.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, CO₂ (or other correct small molecules)
questions.explanation: Small molecules are made of a few non-metal atoms. Do not give diamond or silicon dioxide, which are giant structures.

questions.question: Describe the dot and cross diagram for a hydrogen molecule, H₂.
markScheme: 1 mark: two overlapping circles (outer shells) labelled H
1 mark: one dot and one cross in the overlap (shared pair)
questions.explanation: Each hydrogen atom provides one electron to the shared pair, so each atom has a share of 2 electrons, like helium.

questions.question: Explain why an oxygen molecule, O₂, has a double bond.
markScheme: 1 mark: each oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more for a full shell
1 mark: so the atoms share two pairs of electrons
questions.explanation: Sharing two pairs gives each O 8 outer electrons (4 shared + 2 lone pairs).

questions.question: Describe the dot and cross diagram for a water molecule.
acceptedAnswers: dot and cross in each overlap
markScheme: 1 mark: O outer shell overlapping two H atoms
1 mark: one shared pair (• ×) in each overlap
1 mark: two lone pairs on oxygen (8 outer electrons in total on O)
questions.explanation: Oxygen uses 2 of its 6 electrons to bond with two H atoms; the other 4 form two lone pairs.

questions.question:
Give the molecular formula of a molecule with this displayed formula:
H–C≡C–H
and state the number of shared pairs of electrons between the two carbon atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: C₂H₂
1 mark: 3 shared pairs (a triple bond)
questions.explanation: Count atoms: 2 C, 2 H. ≡ shows a triple bond, which is three shared pairs.

questions.question: Give two limitations of a dot and cross diagram for a molecule of methane.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: does not show the 3D (tetrahedral) shape / bond angles; does not show relative sizes of atoms; suggests electrons from different atoms are different
questions.explanation: Dot and cross diagrams are flat and focus on electrons, so they lose information about shape and size.

questions.question: Explain why the formula SiO₂ does not represent a molecule, whereas CO₂ does.
markScheme: 1 mark: SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure / huge network of atoms, so the formula shows only the ratio of atoms
1 mark: CO₂ is a small molecule containing exactly 1 C and 2 O atoms
questions.explanation: Formulae of giant structures give the simplest ratio; formulae of small molecules give the actual numbers of atoms.

questions.question: Hydrogen sulfide has the formula H₂S. Sulfur is in Group 6. Predict the bonding in H₂S and describe its dot and cross diagram.
markScheme: 1 mark: covalent (both non-metals)
1 mark: one shared pair between S and each H (two in total)
1 mark: two lone pairs on sulfur, giving 8 outer electrons
questions.explanation: Sulfur is in the same group as oxygen, so H₂S is drawn like H₂O.

questions.question: Compare a dot and cross diagram and a ball and stick model as ways of representing an ammonia molecule, NH₃.
markScheme: Indicative content: dot and cross: shows the outer electrons; shows which atom each electron came from; shows 3 shared pairs and the lone pair on N; does not show 3D shape or bond angles; does not show relative sizes. Ball and stick: shows 3D shape (pyramidal) and bond angles; shows which atoms are bonded; does not show electrons or the lone pair; sticks are not real; atoms further apart than in reality.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison giving a strength and a limitation of each representation
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements about one or both representations, with little comparison
questions.explanation: Compare means give similarities or differences for both. The dot and cross diagram is best for electrons; the ball and stick model is best for shape.

questions.question:
Covalently bonded substances can be small molecules, very large molecules or giant covalent structures.
Describe covalent bonding and explain how the bonding is represented in each of these three types of substance, using a named example of each.
markScheme: Indicative content: covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms; strong bond; small molecules e.g. H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, Cl₂: can be shown by dot and cross diagrams with shared pairs in overlaps and lone pairs, or displayed formulae with a line for each bond; very large molecules e.g. poly(ethene): shown as a repeating unit in brackets with n, bonds passing through the brackets, each line a single bond; giant covalent structures e.g. diamond or silicon dioxide: shown as part of a network with lines for bonds, the lines continuing at the edges because the structure is very large; limitations, e.g. diagrams show only part of the structure, do not show 3D shape.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): an accurate description of covalent bonding with correct examples of all three types and clear descriptions of how each is represented
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct description of covalent bonding with examples and representations of at least two types
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements about sharing electrons, with an example or representation of one type
questions.explanation: Use the correct examples from the specification: small molecules (H₂O), polymers (poly(ethene)) and giant covalent (diamond, silicon dioxide). Lines represent single bonds in all three.

questions.question: Explain how the atoms in a methane molecule, CH₄, achieve full outer shells. Your answer should refer to the electronic structures of carbon and hydrogen.
markScheme: Indicative content: carbon is 2,4 and has 4 outer electrons; needs 4 more for a full shell (8); hydrogen has 1 electron and needs 1 more (full shell of 2); carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogen atoms; each shared pair contains one electron from C and one from H; four single covalent bonds; C now has 8 outer electrons and each H has 2.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear explanation linking the electronic structures to the number of shared pairs, with the final electron count for each atom
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'carbon shares electrons with hydrogen', with limited detail
questions.explanation: Carbon needs four electrons and each hydrogen needs one, so four shared pairs satisfy every atom.
